children: By Dalvin Brown and Ashlea Ebeling
Todd and Tiffany Dolci will have about two days next week to pick out their health plans, and they are getting ready for the sprint.

His employer will open enrollment with its new pricing on Nov. 2. Her employer just overhauled its benefits, and allows enrollment until Nov. 4. The couple, who live in the San Francisco Bay Area, will have to compare dozens of combinations of plans with different costs and benefits to cover them and their two children.

Open enrollment is more complicated than ever as healthcare costs rise. Workers pay an average of $7,471 toward family coverage this year, up 9% from last year, according to KFF's annual survey of employers. In the year ahead, nearly half of large employers expect changes that will raise out-of-pocket costs, according to the employee-benefits consulting firm Marsh.
Couples like the Dolcis can end up with higher bills and more unfamiliar choices. They can also face two sets of employer plans that don't lend themselves to neat comparisons.

But the Dolcis have an edge. Todd, 48 years old, is a benefits broker at an insurance firm that advises employers and their employees on their health plans. Tiffany, 45, manages a veterinary hospital. She has chronic conditions that send her to specialists and other doctors more often than anyone else in the family. They are comparing the benefits together — something many couples don't do.
"This conversation rarely happens," Todd said. "What typically happens is they just default to what they've always had."

A life change such as a marriage, divorce, baby or new diagnosis often prompts people to take a fresh look at their benefits. But so should changes in premiums, deductibles, drug coverage or provider networks.

For years, the answer for the Dolcis was easy. When Tiffany's hospital was independently owned, his employer's offerings were always the cheaper option, so the whole family, including their children, now 12 and 7, stayed on his plan.

Last fall, Todd ran the numbers and decided to move the family from his employer's traditional PPO, a preferred-provider organization plan with a low deductible, to its high-deductible plan. Their premiums fell from about $1,350 a month to $595.

The plan lets them put pretax money into a health savings account where unused money rolls over from year to year. And his employer adds $3,000 a year to the account. The balance can be invested and then withdrawn tax-free for medical expenses.

Tiffany had been hesitant, knowing she would pay full price for her specialist visits and medications until the family hit its deductible. "I was like, are you sure?" she said. "But he was pretty sure. So I just went along with it."

The switch cut the family's premiums by about $9,000 this year. It was cheaper, even though Tiffany felt like she was paying more because she spent $5,000 or more at doctors' offices and the pharmacy.

This fall, Tiffany's employer offers four plans: a high-deductible plan, two traditional PPOs and Surest, a unique UnitedHealthcare plan with copays and no deductible for in-network care. Tiffany is leaning toward Surest for only herself, because she sees specialists often and would rather pay a fixed amount for each visit, as she did on their old PPO.
They are deciding whose plan covers them in three steps.

Step One: Find out what each plan costs in premiums. Covering just Tiffany would cost $178 a month on Surest — the plan she is leaning toward. Covering the whole family through her employer would cost between $512 and $1,254 a month. Her cheapest family option costs less than the $595 Todd pays now, but unlike his employer, hers doesn't put money into an HSA.

Step Two: Lay out the options. The family can go three ways: everyone on her plan, everyone on his plan or a split between the two. If she moved the children to her plan, it wouldn't save them money. Any premium savings would be wiped out because his employer's HSA contribution would be cut in half. So the split they are discussing puts Tiffany on Surest and Todd and the children on his high-deductible plan.

Step Three: Estimate what a year would cost, all in, under each option. When Todd's options come in, he will build a spreadsheet, lining up plans with similar deductibles and copays. He tells clients to think about the year ahead, because a new baby or a knee replacement can bring big bills that may make a plan with a lower deductible the cheaper choice.

What the Dolcis will come away with is two numbers. The first is the least they could conceivably pay, which is simply a year of premiums, minus any money the employer puts into a health savings account. The second is roughly the most they will pay: Those premiums plus the plan's yearly limits on what they owe for care, in- and out-of-network.

Tiffany's benefits guide puts her range on Surest next year at about $2,100 to $8,100: $2,136 in premiums plus up to $6,000 for in-network care. Surest covers nothing out of network except emergencies. Todd can't price out next year's high-deductible plan until his new rates arrive. But at this year's rates, to cover himself and the kids, it would cost him between $2,300 and $12,300 after subtracting the money his employer puts in his HSA.

If the enrollment windows barely overlap, start the conversation when the first one opens. It never hurts to ask the employer with the later window for a sneak peek of next year's benefits and costs, though don't be surprised if the answer is no.

Todd ran early math for next year by adjusting higher what he pays now, since his employer sent an email saying premiums will increase slightly. His calculations suggest that, yes, Tiffany should go on her employer's Surest plan, with Todd and the children remaining on his.

At his estimated rates, taking Tiffany off his plan would lower his premium by about $200 a month. With her Surest plan adding $178 a month, the family would pay about $571 a month in all, about $25 less than they pay now. "Not a huge amount of money," he said.
His employer would also put $600 less a year into his HSA.

Tiffany would no longer need to pay out of pocket until she reaches her current $3,400 deductible, because her specialists are in-network under Surest, she said. And if she sees them regularly and keeps filling expensive prescriptions, she could recoup the savings and then some.
Couples should also check:
Spousal rules. Some employers bar a spouse who has access to insurance elsewhere, or charge them more.

Conflicting accounts. A general-purpose health flexible-spending account, or FSA, that covers a spouse makes both spouses ineligible for new Health Savings Account contributions. A limited purpose FSA for vision and dental expenses doesn't create that conflict.
Dental and vision. These are usually separate choices, so a family can take medical coverage from one employer and dental or vision from the other.
Other pretax benefits. Commuter and dependent-care accounts are generally part of open enrollment and can offer meaningful tax savings.
Once Todd's rates arrive, the Dolcis plan to go through both enrollment packets "with a fine-toothed comb," Tiffany said. Last fall, she went along with Todd's math. This time, she plans to weigh in.
"She may not want to listen to me," Todd said.
"If it's cheaper and more convenient for me," Tiffany said, "I will definitely move over to what my company offers."
